text.p: British conglomerate Lonrho Plc on Thursday said it has received interest from potential buyers for its Metropole and Princess hotels and, as a result, is delaying a planned flotation of the properties.

A Lonrho spokesman said both British and overseas parties have expressed interest in the hotels, with some looking at the entire group and others interested in parts of it. He said a decision on the future of the hotels is expected to be made by the end of September.
The spokesman declined to comment on the identity of the bidders.

"The prospectus was due tomorrow, but leading up to this we had a variety of approaches which have hardened to such a degree...as to require a pause in the flotation process," the spokesman said. He said bids were not yet down to final figures.

Analysts said a trade sale of the hotels appeared likely and said a range of British and American hotel operators are likely bidders for the British Metropole chain and the Princess chain of five-star resort hotels.
"At this stage odds are it won't float," said Greg Feehely, a leisure analyst with Kleinwort Benson Securities. "There's a number of interested parties as such that it won't float."
Analysts have estimated that a public offering of the Metropole and Princess hotels would bring a market valuation of about 700 million pounds ($1.10 billion).

Companies that might be interested in acquiring the whole operation include Millennium & Copthorne, whose own portfolio includes hotels in both Britain and the U.S., as well as the U.S.-based chains Marriott, ITT Sheraton and Hilton.

Specialist resort operators in the U.S. might be interested in the Princess hotels, which includes resorts in Acapulco, Mexico, the Caribbean and the U.S. The Metropole might be attractive to UK companies such as Stakis and Bass Plc, operator of the Holiday Inns, said Alex Kyriakidis, an analyst with Arthur Andersen.
The Metropole, which has five locations in London, Birmingham, Brighton and Blackpool, is a four-star chain with extensive conference facilities.
"We wouldn't be surprised if there weren't more interst in the Princess hotels from U.S. companies, -- a company such as Renaissance in the U.S," said Feehely.
Renaissance, operator of the Renaissance, New World and Ramada International hotels, is "...standing at a very high multiple in the U.S.," said Feehely. "That's a good time to do a rights issue.

Other possibilites include a split by Marriott and Whitbread, holder of the Marriott franchise in the UK, under which Marriott would take the Princess hotels and Whitbread take Metropole, Feehely said.

Some analysts said a sale of the hotels would have to carry a premium to the estimated market valuation. But others said Lonrho might be willing to sell at a price close to the market value in order to avoid risk.

"There's a danger that the flotation game is playing itself out," said one analyst. The London stock market has seen a spate of flotations by hotel companies over recent months -- including Millennium & Copthorne, Jarvis Hotels and Macdonald Hotels.
Thistle Hotels, Britain's second largest hotel chain, is due to float within a few weeks.

"They might be worried that if they go for the flotation that it might not be successful," said Ron Littleboy, a Nomura Securities analyst. "It's much cleaner and easier to sell the whole thing. It might be at a discount."
